docs.title: OTA Update Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer / CI
    participant HTTP as Board HTTP Server
    participant Flash as STM32 Flash Driver
    participant MCU as MCUboot (next boot)
    participant App as New Application

    Dev->>HTTP: POST /api/firmware\nAuthorization: Bearer <token>\nContent-Type: application/octet-stream\nBody: zephyr.signed.bin (292 KB)
    HTTP->>HTTP: Validate Content-Length\n(≤ 640 KB)
    HTTP->>HTTP: Lock g_ota_mutex
    HTTP->>Flash: flash_img_init_id(slot1_partition)
    loop 4 KB chunks
        HTTP->>Flash: flash_img_buffered_write(chunk, flush)
        Note over Flash: IMG_ERASE_PROGRESSIVELY:\nerase sector on first write to it
    end
    HTTP->>Flash: boot_request_upgrade(BOOT_UPGRADE_TEST)
    Note over Flash: Sets swap magic in slot1 trailer
    HTTP-->>Dev: {"status":"ok","bytes":292772}
    HTTP->>HTTP: Unlock g_ota_mutex

    Dev->>HTTP: POST /api/reboot\nAuthorization: Bearer <token>
    HTTP-->>Dev: {"status":"rebooting"}
    HTTP->>HTTP: zsock_close → k_msleep(200)\n→ sys_reboot(COLD)

    MCU->>Flash: Read slot1 swap magic → perform swap
    MCU->>MCU: Verify ECDSA-P256 signature
    alt Signature valid
        MCU->>App: Chainload new application
        App->>Flash: boot_write_img_confirmed()\n→ marks image_ok
        App->>App: Normal operation
    else Signature invalid or image corrupt
        MCU->>Flash: Restore previous image from scratch
        MCU->>App: Chainload previous application
    end

docs.title: Rollback Mechanism
docs.text:
MCUboot uses test-mode swap (BOOT_UPGRADE_TEST):

  1. After upload, the slot1 trailer contains a swap magic marker but image_ok = 0.
  2. On the next boot, MCUboot sees the magic, swaps slot1 → slot0, then boots the new image.
  3. The new image must call boot_write_img_confirmed() before the watchdog fires.
  4. If the new image crashes before confirming (hard fault, stack overflow, watchdog reset), MCUboot sees image_ok = 0 on the subsequent boot and automatically swaps back to the previous image.

This means a corrupt or incompatible OTA binary cannot permanently brick the board.

docs.title: Why we override partitions
docs.text: The board's default nucleo_h753zi.dts defines slot0 as 256 KB — smaller than our 286 KB app binary. The overlay expands slots to 640 KB each while preserving the original node names to avoid DTS unit-address warnings.

docs.title: Key lesson: MCUboot needs chosen override
docs.text:
The board DTS has zephyr,code-partition = &slot0_partition in the chosen node. Without an explicit override in sysbuild/mcuboot.overlay, MCUboot links itself to slot0 (0x08040000) — and the app write overwrites the bootloader.

Fix in sysbuild/mcuboot.overlay: 

/ {
    chosen {
        zephyr,code-partition = &boot_partition;
    };
};

This forces MCUboot to link to boot_partition (0x08000000, 128 KB), not slot0.

docs.title: Kconfig Summary
docs.text: Option Value Purpose CONFIG_BOOTLOADER_MCUBOOT y App linked to slot0, includes MCUboot header CONFIG_IMG_MANAGER y boot_request_upgrade(), boot_write_img_confirmed() CONFIG_FLASH_MAP y Flash area abstraction CONFIG_STREAM_FLASH y Streaming write API for OTA CONFIG_IMG_ERASE_PROGRESSIVELY y Sector erased on first write — no full pre-erase needed CONFIG_BOOT_SIGNATURE_TYPE_ECDSA_P256 y (MCUboot) Signature algorithm CONFIG_BOOT_MAX_IMG_SECTORS 512 Max sectors per slot MCUboot manages

docs.title: Build & Flash Commands
docs.text:
Initial flash (JTAG, both MCUboot + app): 

cd /home/baloo/zephyrproject
rm -rf build
west build -b nucleo_h753zi /path/to/zephyr --sysbuild
west flash

Subsequent updates (OTA, no JTAG needed): 

# After building a new signed app:
TOKEN=$(grep -oP '(?<=")[0-9a-f]{64}' zephyr/src/http/http_auth.hpp)
curl -X POST http://192.168.1.80/api/firmware \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/octet-stream" \
     --data-binary @build/zephyr/zephyr/zephyr.signed.bin
curl -X POST http://192.168.1.80/api/reboot -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

Verify OTA succeeded (UART): 

[MCUBOOT] Bootloader chainload address offset: 0x40000
[MCUBOOT] Jumping to the first image slot
[00:00:00.xxx] <inf> hdv_sim: Phase : 3b - OTA firmware update
[00:00:00.xxx] <inf> hdv_sim: BOOT: image confirmed OK

docs.title: MQTT(S) Control — Implementation Plan
docs.text: Add an MQTT(S) subscriber on the STM32 that accepts actuator commands from an external broker (Mosquitto on Pi or cloud). The web dashboard gets a toggle to switch the active control source between CAN and MQTT.

docs.title: g_cmd source arbitration
docs.text:
The cleanest approach reuses the existing g_cmd / g_cmd_mutex pattern. The MQTT subscriber decodes incoming messages and writes to g_cmd exactly as the CAN RX thread does. The plant thread is unaware of the source.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                          │
│  CAN RX thread    ──┐                                    │
│                     ├─→ g_cmd_mutex → g_cmd             │
│  MQTT RX thread   ──┘        ↑                          │
│                               │                          │
│  HTTP /dash?...  ─────────────┘  (apply_web_cmd)        │
│                                                          │
│  Control source:  g_ctrl_source (atomic)                 │
│    CAN_SOURCE | MQTT_SOURCE | HTTP_SOURCE                │
│                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Source arbitration — Option A (recommended, least code):

Each source writes g_cmd independently. The existing CAN watchdog resets commands if no fresh CAN frame arrives in 500 ms — add an equivalent MQTT watchdog. The dashboard toggle just enables/disables which thread is allowed to write.

Option B (explicit g_ctrl_source atomic enum) adds more control but is only needed if sources must be hard-locked out from each other.

docs.text: tls_creds_init() already loads the server cert + key into HDV_TLS_SERVER_TAG = 1. For MQTT connecting to an external broker, the STM32 acts as a TLS client. docs.title: Security Hardening — Implementation Reference
docs.text:
Signing algorithm in the built images

This page describes ECDSA-P256, which is what sysbuild/mcuboot.conf requests. Sysbuild overrides it: the images actually built and verified use RSA-2048 with MCUboot's test key (root-rsa-2048.pem). See MCUboot signing & flash recovery and Build, Flash & OTA. The slot0 / slot1 size is 640 KB.

STM32H753ZI / Nucleo-H753ZI — Phases 1 through 3b

docs.text:

docs.title: Phase Summary
docs.text: Phase Control Threat Mitigated 1 HTTP Bearer token (64-char hex) Unauthenticated command injection via HTTP 1 Session cookie (32-char hex, 1h TTL) Browser session hijack after login 2 IWDG hardware watchdog (1s timeout, 5s reset) Firmware hang / infinite loop 2 SYS_INIT early kicks (PRE_KERNEL_1 → APPLICATION) Watchdog firing during boot before threads start 3a MCUboot ECDSA-P256 signature check Unsigned or tampered firmware execution 3a Dual-slot with test-mode swap Bricking from failed OTA 3b OTA auth (Bearer required for /api/firmware) Unauthenticated firmware replacement 3b Signed-binary-only OTA Attacker pushing unsigned replacement via OTA 4 (planned) RDP Level 1 Flash readback / firmware extraction via SWD

docs.title: Token model
docs.text:
Deployment time:
  scripts/gen_http_token.sh  →  http_auth.hpp (gitignored)
  Content: #define HTTP_BEARER_TOKEN "5f580d6c..."  (64 hex chars = 256-bit entropy)

Runtime:
  POST /login  body: token=<value>
       │
       ├─ verify_bearer() — constant-time strncmp + length check
       │        │
       │    success ──► session_create() → 32-char hex token → Set-Cookie: sid=...
       │    failure ──► send_login_page(bad_token=true) — no timing side-channel
       │
  GET /dash   Cookie: sid=<token>
       │
       └─ session_check() → scan 4-slot table, compare token, check TTL

docs.title: Remaining exposure (HTTP, no TLS)
docs.text:
• Token and session cookie travel in plaintext → passive LAN observer can capture and replay
  • Mitigated by: isolated lab/LAN environment; HTTPS (planned next) eliminates this

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
Power-on
  │
  ├─ PRE_KERNEL_1  iwdg_early_kick() ─ AAAAH kick (counter reset, no PR/RLR write)
  ├─ PRE_KERNEL_2  iwdg_early_kick() ─ AAAAH kick
  ├─ POST_KERNEL   iwdg_early_kick() ─ AAAAH kick
  ├─ APPLICATION   iwdg_early_kick() ─ AAAAH kick
  │
  ├─ watchdog_thread (priority 2) starts
  │     wdt_install_timeout(window.max=1000ms)
  │     wdt_setup(PAUSE_HALTED_BY_DBG)
  │     PR=6, RLR=624 → 5s hardware timeout programmed
  │
  │     ┌── Grace period (10 s): feed every 500 ms ─────────────────┐
  │     │   allows all threads to start and stabilise               │
  │     └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  └─ Monitoring phase: k_sem_take(g_wdt_sem, K_MSEC(500))
        ├─ sem given by plant_thread every step (10 ms)  → wdt_feed() → loop
        └─ sem NOT given within 500 ms → watchdog expires → SoC reset

docs.title: Why IWDG over WWDG
docs.text: IWDG runs on LSI (independent clock — not affected by main clock failures). WWDG runs on PCLK1 (gated by the clock tree). A firmware hang that disrupts the main clock tree will stop WWDG but not IWDG.

docs.title: Root cause of original boot loop
docs.text: At 52 ms boot time: IWDG was inherited from a previous session (not cleared by warm reset) with a short timeout. Early Zephyr boot phases have no thread scheduler, so wdt_feed() could not run. Fixed by direct register kicks (0xAAAA to KR) at each SYS_INIT level.

docs.title: Signature verification
docs.text:
MCUboot image layout (slot0 starting at 0x08040000):
┌─────────────────────────────────┐ ← 0x08040000
│  MCUboot image header  (512 B)  │  magic, version, img_size, flags
├─────────────────────────────────┤ ← 0x08040200
│                                 │
│  Application binary             │  Zephyr RTOS + all threads
│  (~285 KB)                      │
│                                 │
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│  TLV Info header                │  type=SHA256, type=ECDSA_SIG
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│  SHA-256 hash of image region   │  32 bytes
│  ECDSA-P256 signature           │  64 bytes (r, s)
│  Key hash                       │  32 bytes (SHA-256 of public key)
└─────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Partition isolation
docs.text: MCUboot occupies sector 0 (0x08000000–0x0801FFFF). The app starts at sector 2 (0x08040000). Flashing slot0 erases sectors 2–6; it cannot reach sector 0. MCUboot survives an app flash.

docs.title: Auth chain for OTA
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    DEV[Developer] -->|POST /api/firmware\nAuthorization: Bearer TOKEN| HTTP
    HTTP --> VERIFY{verify_bearer\nor session_check}
    VERIFY -- fail --> R401[401 Unauthorized\nno flash write]
    VERIFY -- pass --> SIZE{Content-Length\n≤ 640 KB?}
    SIZE -- no --> R413[413 Content Too Large]
    SIZE -- yes --> MUTEX{g_ota_mutex\navailable?}
    MUTEX -- locked --> R503[503 Service Unavailable]
    MUTEX -- free --> WRITE[flash_img_buffered_write\n→ slot1]
    WRITE --> ARM[boot_request_upgrade\nBOOT_UPGRADE_TEST]
    ARM --> R200[200 OK\nbytes written]
    R200 --> REBOOT[POST /api/reboot]
    REBOOT --> MCUBOOT[MCUboot verifies\nECDSA-P256 signature]
    MCUBOOT -- invalid --> ROLLBACK[Rollback to\nprevious image]
    MCUBOOT -- valid --> NEWAPP[New app boots\nboot_write_img_confirmed]

docs.title: Phase 4 Preview — RDP Level 1
docs.text:
Not yet applied. Applied as the absolute last step before production.

RDP Level 1 sets STM32's RDP option byte to 0xBB: - SWD/JTAG can still halt the CPU and program flash — development workflow unchanged - SWD/JTAG cannot read back flash contents — firmware extraction blocked - ROM UART bootloader can write new firmware but cannot read back - Downgrading to RDP Level 0 triggers a full mass erase — all flash wiped

After RDP Level 1, OTA (Phase 3b) becomes the primary in-field update mechanism.

docs.title: Web UI & HTTP API
docs.text: The board serves its own dashboard over HTTPS (https://192.168.1.80). The UI is a small TypeScript single-page app built with Vite, embedded in the firmware image at build time. No file system, no external server, and no framework: the whole bundle is about 17 KB.

docs.title: What the dashboard shows
docs.text:
Card Content Source Vehicle motion Speed, state of charge, yaw rate, vx / vy / yaw / x / y / steer, wheel speeds, surface μ /api/state Actuator command Enable, gear, torque, brake, steer as seen by the plant /api/state CAN TX / RX frames, timeouts, time of last RX /api/state Controls Stop, Drive FWD / REV, steer ±5°, manual inject form /dash?… Control source CAN / MQTT / HTTP selector, MQTT broker address and port /dash?… System Heap use, free heap, worst-case simulation loop time /api/state Kernel threads Priority and stack use per thread /api/system Memory map Flash (slot0) and RAM image footprint, heap pools, stacks /api/system Vehicle Mass, battery, motor power / torque, max speed, gear ratio static

There is also an OTA view (/ota) for uploading firmware. See Build, Flash & OTA.

docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph repo["Repository"]
        TS["webui/src/*.ts<br/>TypeScript + Vite"]
        DIST["webui/dist/<br/>index.html, app.js, app.css"]
    end
    subgraph fw["Firmware image"]
        INC["webui_*.inc<br/>(generate_inc_file_for_target)"]

    BR["Browser"]

    TS -- "npm run build" --> DIST
    DIST -- "CMake embeds" --> INC

  • The UI polls /api/state every 2 s and /api/system every 5 s.
  • A request that returns 401 sends the browser back to the login page.

docs.title: HTTP API
docs.text:
All endpoints except the login page and the static assets require authentication: either a valid session cookie (sid=…, set by POST /login) or Authorization: Bearer <token>.

Method Path Auth Response GET /, /login no Login page POST /login no token=<hex> body; sets session cookie, redirects to /dash GET /logout no Invalidates the session, redirects to / GET /app.js, /app.css no Embedded UI assets (contain no secrets) GET /dash yes UI shell (index.html) GET /dash?<params> yes Applies the command, returns 204 GET /ota yes UI shell, OTA view GET /api/state yes Plant, command, CAN and MQTT telemetry (JSON) GET /api/system yes Threads, memory map, MQTT broker settings (JSON) POST /api/firmware yes Raw zephyr.signed.bin body, streamed to slot1 POST /api/reboot yes Cold reboot into MCUboot to apply the update

docs.title: Command parameters (GET /dash?…)
docs.text:
Parameter Values Effect steer −45 … 45 (°) Steering command torque 0 … 145000 (Nm) Drive torque brake 0 … 100 (%) Brake command gear F, R, N Gear selector enable 0, 1 System enable ctrl can, mqtt, http Active control source (names, not numbers) broker_addr, broker_port string / 1 … 65535 MQTT broker; triggers a reconnect

Values are clamped to physical limits in apply_web_cmd() before they reach g_cmd.

Command source and watchdog

Only the active control source can write g_cmd. Commands sent while the source is not http are decoded and discarded. In addition, the plant resets any command that has not been refreshed for 500 ms (CAN_RX_TIMEOUT_S). The dashboard therefore resends the active command every 300 ms while the HTTP source is selected, and releases it on Stop or when the source changes. Scripts that talk to /dash?… directly must do the same.

docs.title: Developing the UI
docs.text:
Node 18 or newer is enough (the project pins Vite 5).

cd webui
npm ci
npm run dev        # http://localhost:5173, served against a built-in mock board

The mock (mock-api.ts) implements /api/state, /api/system, /api/firmware, /api/reboot and the command parameters, so the whole UI, including the OTA view, can be exercised without hardware. To point the dev server at a real board instead:

HDV_PROXY=https://192.168.1.80 HDV_COOKIE="sid=<session cookie>" npm run dev

Dev server ≠ production bundle

The dev server loads modules lazily; the firmware serves one bundled file. Check the production bundle (npm run build) on the board before relying on a change.

npm run build type-checks (tsc --noEmit) and writes webui/dist/. CMake refuses to build the firmware if index.html, app.js or app.css is missing from dist/. scripts/ota_flash.sh builds the UI first.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: Constraint Detail One request at a time http_tid is a single thread. Every request is a new TLS connection (Connection: close) with an ECDHE-RSA handshake. TLS contexts Listen (1) + accepted (2) + MQTTS client (1) + headroom (1). Image budget The UI adds about 17 KB of flash (not compressed in the image). Assets are public /app.js and /app.css need no login; never put secrets in the UI source.

docs.title: Planned: WebSocket transport
docs.text: Not implemented yet. Because of the constraints above, polling and per-command connections cost a TLS handshake each. The plan is one persistent WebSocket for telemetry push and command input, which would also remove the per-command handshake from the 300 ms command hold. A related project, embedded_sim, already serves telemetry over a WebSocket (/ws) from Zephyr's HTTP server; this firmware uses a hand-written socket server, so the upgrade handshake and framing would have to be added there. The handshake overhead has not been measured on this board, so treat the improvement as unconfirmed until it is.

docs.title: Zephyr — Build, Flash & UART Reference
docs.text: Target: STM32H753ZI (Nucleo-H753ZI) cross-compiled from Raspberry Pi 5 (Ubuntu 24.04 arm64).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Current workflow

The paths and commands on this page are the original Raspberry Pi 5 setup (~/zephyrproject, SDK 0.17). The firmware now needs a Zephyr v3.7.0 workspace, builds the web UI first, and is normally flashed over the network. See Build, Flash & OTA for the current steps; this page remains useful for the shell command list and UART troubleshooting.

West workspace must already be initialised at ~/zephyrproject and the Zephyr SDK installed at ~/zephyr-sdk-0.17.0. See docs/ZEPHYR_RPI5_SETUP.md for the one-time setup.

Activate the venv before any west command:

source ~/zephyrproject/.venv/bin/activate

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
cd ~/zephyrproject
west build -b nucleo_h753zi /home/baloo/repos/vehicle-Dynamics-Sim-Can/zephyr

Clean build (required when switching phases, board configs, or Kconfig):

rm -rf ~/zephyrproject/build
west build -b nucleo_h753zi /home/baloo/repos/vehicle-Dynamics-Sim-Can/zephyr

Memory usage is printed at the end of a successful build:

Memory region    Used Size   Region Size   %age Used
           FLASH:      99040 B         2 MB      4.72%
             RAM:      11072 B       512 KB      2.11%

docs.title: Flash
docs.text:
Connect the Nucleo board via CN1 (ST-Link USB) — the USB connector near the ethernet jack, labelled ST-LINK on the PCB. Do not use CN13 (user USB).

west flash

OpenOCD will print read_memory warnings during init — these are non-fatal quirks with OpenOCD 0.11 and STM32H7. Flash succeeds when you see:

wrote XXXXX bytes from file zephyr.hex in X.XXXs
shutdown command invoked

docs.title: Serial Monitor (UART Shell)
docs.text:
The board exposes a virtual COM port over the same ST-Link USB cable.

Find the device:

ls /dev/ttyACM*
# typically /dev/ttyACM0

Connect:

picocom -b 115200 /dev/ttyACM0

Exit: Ctrl+A then Ctrl+X

docs.title: If the port is busy
docs.text:
A previous session may still hold the device:

lsof /dev/ttyACM0        # find the PID
kill <PID>               # release it
# or
screen -wipe             # clean up all detached screen sessions

sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER
# log out and back in, then reconnect

The board silkscreen labels the CAN pins on the CN11 morpho connector (left header). Both CN11 morpho and CN9 ZIO expose the same PD0/PD1 GPIOs — use whichever is more convenient for your transceiver wiring.

An external CAN transceiver is required (e.g. TCAN1042 or SN65HVD230 — both 3.3V compatible). FDCAN2 (PB12/PB13) is available if a second bus is needed.

docs.title: 1a — Logging shim (utils/logging.hpp)
docs.text:
The host LOG_* macros are mapped to Zephyr's structured log backend via a compile-time branch. The shared plant/CAN source files require zero changes.

#ifdef __ZEPHYR__
#include <zephyr/logging/log.h>
// Each .cpp must have LOG_MODULE_REGISTER (one) or LOG_MODULE_DECLARE (others)
#define LOG_TRACE(...) LOG_DBG(__VA_ARGS__)
#define LOG_DEBUG(...) LOG_DBG(__VA_ARGS__)
#define LOG_INFO(...)  LOG_INF(__VA_ARGS__)
#define LOG_WARN(...)  LOG_WRN(__VA_ARGS__)
#define LOG_ERROR(...) LOG_ERR(__VA_ARGS__)
#else
// ... existing host implementation unchanged ...
#endif

Pitfall: LOG_MODULE_REGISTER must appear in exactly one .cpp per module (it is in main.cpp). Every other .cpp that uses the macros needs LOG_MODULE_DECLARE(hdv_sim, LOG_LEVEL_INF).

Pitfall: Zephyr compiles C++ with -nostdinc++. Use C headers (<stdlib.h>, <stdio.h>) not C++ wrappers (<cstdlib>, <cstdio>). Remove unused C++ stdlib includes from shared headers.

Pitfall: nullptr in Zephyr shell macros (SHELL_CMD, SHELL_CMD_REGISTER) causes a C++ type error — use NULL instead.

docs.title: Generator script
docs.text:
tools/gen_can_map.py reads config/can_map.dbc and outputs zephyr/src/can/can_map_static.hpp:

# Usage (from repo root):
python3 tools/gen_can_map.py
# → writes zephyr/src/can/can_map_static.hpp

The generated header defines two plain structs and flat static const arrays — no heap, no std::string:

namespace can_static {
struct SigDef  { const char* name; int16_t start_bit; uint8_t bit_len;
                 bool little_endian; bool is_signed; float factor; float offset; };
struct FrameDef{ uint32_t id; bool is_extended; bool is_rx; uint16_t cycle_ms;
                 uint8_t dlc; const char* name; const SigDef* sigs; uint8_t sig_count; };

static const FrameDef k_frames[16] = { /* 1 RX + 15 TX, all 65 signals */ };

inline const FrameDef* find_rx_frame(uint32_t id);   // linear search < 1 µs on M7
inline const FrameDef* find_tx_frame(uint32_t id);
inline const FrameDef* tx_frame_at(uint8_t idx);
} // namespace can_static

docs.title: ACTUATOR_CMD_1 inline decoder
docs.text:
// Intel byte order (LSB-first), signal positions from can_map.dbc:
c.system_enable       = (d[0] >> 0) & 0x01;
c.gear_position       = static_cast<GearPosition>((d[0] >> 1) & 0x03);
c.steer_cmd_deg       = (int16_t)(d[1] | (d[2] << 8)) * 0.1;
c.drive_torque_cmd_nm = (int16_t)(d[3] | (d[4] << 8)) * 10.0;
c.brake_cmd_pct       = d[5] * 1.0;

docs.title: Timer-driven plant thread
docs.text:
// plant/plant_thread.cpp — prio 5, 16384 B stack
K_SEM_DEFINE(plant_sem, 0, 1);
static void plant_timer_expiry(struct k_timer*) { k_sem_give(&plant_sem); }
K_TIMER_DEFINE(plant_timer, plant_timer_expiry, NULL);
K_THREAD_DEFINE(plant_tid, 16384, plant_thread, NULL, NULL, NULL, 5, 0, 0);

static void plant_thread(void*, void*, void*) {
    LOG_INF("[plant] Heavy-Duty Electric Vehicle plant thread started (dt=10 ms, prio=5)");
    k_timer_start(&plant_timer, K_MSEC(10), K_MSEC(10));

    while (true) {
        k_sem_take(&plant_sem, K_FOREVER);
        const double t_s = k_uptime_get_32() / 1000.0;

        // CAN watchdog: zero command if no RX for 500 ms
        sim::ActuatorCmd cmd;
        k_mutex_lock(&g_cmd_mutex, K_FOREVER);
        cmd = g_cmd;
        k_mutex_unlock(&g_cmd_mutex);
        if ((t_s - g_last_rx_t) > 0.5) {
            cmd = sim::ActuatorCmd{};   // safe-mode: coast with no drive/brake
        }

        // Step physics (10 ms)
        plant::PlantState local_state;
        k_mutex_lock(&g_state_mutex, K_FOREVER);
        local_state = g_state;
        k_mutex_unlock(&g_state_mutex);

        s_plant.step(local_state, cmd, DT_S);

        k_mutex_lock(&g_state_mutex, K_FOREVER);
        g_state = local_state;
        k_mutex_unlock(&g_state_mutex);

        // Brake diagnostics: log every 100 ms while brake > 1%
        if (cmd.brake_cmd_pct > 1.0) { /* LOG_INF("[brk] ... "); */ }

        // CAN TX: pack all sensor frames
        can_tx_send_all(local_state, t_s, loop_us);
    }
}

Superseded

The Controls and Kernel Threads cards below were later rebuilt in the TypeScript UI (Web UI & HTTP API). Commands are now refreshed by the browser every 300 ms because of the 500 ms command watchdog.

The HTTP dashboard was extended with two new cards:

docs.title: CAN watchdog / safe-mode
docs.text: If no ACTUATOR_CMD_1 is received for 500 ms, the plant thread substitutes a zeroed ActuatorCmd (no torque, no brake, neutral gear). This prevents the vehicle from running away if the controller disconnects. The g_can_timeout_count counter is visible on the dashboard under CAN Stats.

docs.title: Brake diagnostics logging
docs.text:
Every 100 ms while braking (brake_cmd_pct > 1), the plant thread emits: 

[brk] t=12.34 vx=8.320 a=-5.91 Fx=-1291kN tau=-2500kNm mode=dyn
[brk] omega FL=4.31 FR=4.31 RL=4.31 RR=4.31 ref=4.31 rad/s
This lets you verify that the Dugoff model is building slip correctly and that a_long matches the expected ~0.6 g braking.

docs.title: Observations
docs.text:
• Ample headroom: 235 KB used of 1 MB — 765 KB free. No trimming required.
  • 128 KB heap dominates the Zephyr kernel entry. If RAM needs saving, reduce CONFIG_HEAP_MEM_POOL_SIZE in prj.conf (e.g. to 64 KB); the TCP + STL allocators will still fit.
  • Net buffers are the next cost at ~22 KB. Can be reduced by lowering CONFIG_NET_PKT_RX_COUNT / CONFIG_NET_BUF_RX_COUNT if the HTTP server is the only consumer.
  • ETH DMA lives in dedicated SRAM (0x30040000) — not counted against the main AXI budget.
  • g_state (560 B) is the largest single application object; its layout is fixed by the physics model struct.

docs.title: Zephyr RTOS — Development Setup on Raspberry Pi 5 (Ubuntu Server 24, arm64)
docs.text: Target: cross-compile Zephyr for STM32 (arm-zephyr-eabi) from an RPi 5 running Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS (aarch64).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Raspberry Pi 5 with Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS (64-bit) installed
  • Internet connection
  • At least 8 GB free disk space (Zephyr + modules + SDK)

docs.title: 1. Update the system
docs.text: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

docs.title: 2. Install system dependencies
docs.text:
sudo apt install -y \
    git cmake ninja-build gperf ccache dfu-util \
    python3-dev python3-pip python3-venv python3-setuptools \
    xz-utils file libpython3-dev libsdl2-dev \
    wget curl unzip

docs.title: 3. Create a dedicated workspace folder
docs.text:
mkdir -p ~/zephyrproject
cd ~/zephyrproject

docs.title: 4. Create and activate a Python venv
docs.text:
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install --upgrade pip

docs.title: 5. Install West
docs.text:
pip install west
west --version   # verify: "West version: v1.x.x"

docs.title: 6. Initialize the West workspace with Zephyr v3.7.0
docs.text:
west init -m https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr --mr v3.7.0 .
west update      # downloads ~1.5 GB — takes 5-10 min on good connection

docs.title: 7. Install Zephyr's Python requirements
docs.text: pip install -r ~/zephyrproject/zephyr/scripts/requirements.txt

docs.title: 8. Download the Zephyr SDK (arm64 minimal)
docs.text:
cd ~/Downloads
wget https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/sdk-ng/releases/download/v0.17.0/zephyr-sdk-0.17.0_linux-aarch64_minimal.tar.xz
tar xf zephyr-sdk-0.17.0_linux-aarch64_minimal.tar.xz -C ~/

docs.title: 9. Install the ARM Cortex-M toolchain
docs.text:
cd ~/zephyr-sdk-0.17.0
./setup.sh -t arm-zephyr-eabi -h

The -h flag installs host tools (CMake modules, Ninja integration). Verify:

~/zephyr-sdk-0.17.0/arm-zephyr-eabi/bin/arm-zephyr-eabi-gcc --version
# arm-zephyr-eabi-gcc (Zephyr SDK 0.17.0) 12.2.0

docs.title: 10. Set environment variables (add to ~/.bashrc)
docs.text:
echo 'export ZEPHYR_SDK_INSTALL_DIR=$HOME/zephyr-sdk-0.17.0' >> ~/.bashrc
echo 'source $HOME/zephyrproject/.venv/bin/activate' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc

docs.title: 11. Build the Zephyr hello_world sample for nucleo_h753zi
docs.text:
cd ~/zephyrproject
west build -b nucleo_h753zi zephyr/samples/basic/hello_world

Expected output at the end: 

Memory region    Used Size   Region Size   %age Used
         FLASH:     ...

docs.title: 12. Flash to the STM32 board (board connected via USB)
docs.text:
# Install OpenOCD
sudo apt install -y openocd

# Flash
west flash

For the Nucleo-H753ZI, connect the CN1 ST-Link USB port to the RPi 5 USB port.

docs.title: 13. Monitor serial output
docs.text:
# Find the VCP device (usually ttyACM0)
ls /dev/ttyACM*

# Open serial monitor at 115200 baud
screen /dev/ttyACM0 115200
# exit: Ctrl+A then K then Y

Expected output: 

*** Booting Zephyr OS build v3.7.0 ***
Hello World! nucleo_h753zi

docs.title: 14. Build your own app instead of the sample
docs.text:
cd ~/zephyrproject
west build -b nucleo_h753zi /path/to/your/zephyr/app
west flash
